summary: Two topics: First, deriving from 'He shall take two goats' the requirement that the pair be matched, and then working through the 'point of no return' principle - after blood sprinkling the sin-offering's atonement is secured; after dispatch the Azazel goat's atonement is secured. Each goat has its own independent critical stage. Second, what happens when the HP slaughters both goats: the lottery designation is binding and cannot be overridden; only the goat designated 'for God' can serve as the sin-offering.

display.whats: 'He shall take two goats': the matching requirement and rules for when one goat fails
display.hint: The verse 'He shall take two goats' requires the pair be matched in appearance and value. The Gemara then details what happens when one goat dies or is invalidated at various stages of the service.
display.title: Matching Requirements and Points of No Return for the Two Goats

learning.ahaMoment: The two Yom Kippur goats are not just paired by convenience - they are a legal unity. What happens to one affects the other. The service has clear points of no return: past the blood sprinkling (sin-offering) and past the dispatch (Azazel), each goat's atonement is secured.
learning.memoryAnchor: Two goats, one service, distinct points of no return: understanding when each goat's atonement is secured is the key to the replacement laws.
learning.learnerQuestion: What physical properties must the two Yom Kippur goats share, and at what point in the service does each goat become irreversibly committed to its designated role?
learning.coreTension: The pairing requirement emphasizes the two goats as a unit, yet each has a distinct role and a different service endpoint; understanding when each is fully committed to its role determines how to handle mid-service failures.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara establishes that the goats must match in appearance, height, and value and be acquired together - though post-facto differences do not invalidate - and then maps the distinct points of no return at each service stage, allowing targeted recovery from mid-stage failures rather than full restart.

takeaway.text: The two Yom Kippur goats must match in appearance, height, and value and be acquired together, though post-facto differences discovered during service do not invalidate; the Gemara maps distinct points of no return at different service stages, enabling targeted recovery from mid-stage failures.

learning.learningBlocker: Students may assume matching is a strict invalidating requirement at all stages; they miss the distinction between the initial acquisition requirement and post-facto tolerance, as well as the staged points of no return that determine what recovery is possible.

display.title: The Lottery is Binding: Divine Designation Cannot Be Reversed

learning.ahaMoment: The lottery is not a formality - it creates binding legal status. The HP cannot unilaterally alter which goat plays which role, and slaughtering both is a fundamental violation of the service.
learning.memoryAnchor: The lottery is binding: not even the HP can override it by slaughtering the Azazel goat instead of dispatching it.
learning.learnerQuestion: If the HP slaughters both Yom Kippur goats or slaughters them in reverse order, does the lottery designation remain binding or is it effectively overridden by the physical act?
learning.coreTension: The lottery physically assigns each goat to its role; one might think that if the HP slaughters both or reverses the order, the practical outcome (one goat's blood sprinkled, one dispatched) could be treated as valid since the physical acts were performed.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara rules the lottery is absolutely binding: only the goat designated 'for God' by the lottery may serve as the sin-offering regardless of the HP's subsequent actions; slaughtering the Azazel goat or reversing the order produces an invalid service because the lottery is an act of divine designation, not a practical label subject to human reversal.

takeaway.text: The lottery designation is binding and cannot be overridden by the HP's subsequent actions; only the goat designated 'for God' may serve as the sin-offering, and slaughtering the wrong goat or reversing the order invalidates the service - the lottery is divine designation, not a practical label.

learning.learningBlocker: Students may think of the lottery as a practical selection mechanism that assigns roles flexibly; they miss that the lottery is a formal act of divine designation that locks each goat into its specific role with no room for human reversal.

rashiTranslations.en: 'Gemara: from where do we derive that it is indispensable' - if you might say because the indispensable decree is written regarding it, but according to both Rabbi Yehuda
and Rabbi Nechemya, the decree is written only regarding acts that are part of the service itself,
but not regarding the taking of the animals, which happens the day before. 'You might have thought "two," "two," "two"' -
the word is written three times, and Scripture repeated it to make it indispensable. 'One for appearance,' etc. - and this teaches a mitzvah,
not something indispensable. 'It is written "shall be"' - 'this shall be'
'the law of the metzora,' which implies that in its ongoing state
this passage shall remain in force exactly as all that is written in it.
'For a mitzvah, do we likewise require' - that they be
equal to each other? But did we not teach this same requirement regarding the daily offerings?
'Corresponding to the day' - corresponding to the rising of the sun.
'Or is it perhaps only an obligation of the day' - and it comes to teach
that there shall be two lambs for each day. 'At the northwest
corner' - of the altar, since the sun rises from
the east, therefore the slaughterer draws the animal toward
the west, to keep it away from the eastern wall,
as far as possible, because the walls are high
and in the early morning the sun is still low on the horizon,
so the wall's shadow stands directly against it; and it is the north side
because most-holy offerings are slaughtered at
the north side of the altar's base, where the slaughtering-house
stood, and the rings were fixed into the floor
to hold the animal's head, twenty
four of them corresponding to the number of the priestly watches, occupying an area
of twenty-four by twenty
four cubits, arranged in six rows. 'At the second
ring' - not the ring nearest
the altar, but the one next to it, drawn toward
the north, with the slaughterer's face and the animal's neck
angled toward the northeast, from where
the morning sun rises; and the reason for the ring
being specifically the second one I do not know myself, but I have heard it is so that
the first ring may help hold
the animal's legs so it does not overturn. And for the afternoon offering,
since the sun comes from the west,
he draws himself as far as possible toward the east,
with his face toward the southwest, angled toward where the rising
of the sun comes from. 'And the Sabbath additional offerings' -
regarding which it says 'two lambs,' certainly meaning two
equal lambs, indispensably, since it does not go on to write regarding them
'one' a second time to include validity even when they are not equal -
so I have heard it, but I find it difficult, since it should say from where do we derive it is indispensable;
and it appears to me that the correct reading is: the additional offerings
certainly require two lambs as a mitzvah, meaning their proper observance is to be equal,
and we do not read it as 'since it does not write one, one' -
that alternate reading belongs to the school of the students of the academy.
'The two goats of Yom Kippur' - which from the moment they were acquired
are sanctified, since they came from the terumah of the treasury chamber,
and he slaughtered them outside the Temple courtyard. 'He is liable for
both of them' - on account of slaughtering outside; and later the Gemara will ask:
before the lottery, for what purpose are they fit to be offered inside? And since
they are not yet fit, why is he liable? We require that they be fit to be brought to the entrance of
the Tent of Meeting, as it is written (Leviticus 17)
regarding those slaughtered outside, 'and he did not bring it to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting.'
'But he is exempt regarding the one for Azazel' -
since it is not fit to be offered inside at all. 'For the goat
offered outside' - meaning each of the two was fit
to be offered as the additional sin-offering goat of
Yom Kippur stated in the portion of Pinchas.
'And why is it different regarding the goat offered inside, that it is not' -

fit? Because it still lacks the lottery. 'They are also not fit for the goat offered outside' - since they still lack the entire day's service: the placing of the blood of the bull and the goat, and the scooping of the incense and its burning,

all of which are meant to precede the additional offerings. 'There is no lack of time within the day itself' - regarding the outer goat, there is no lack of an act performed on its own body, only a lack of time, since the time has not yet arrived

for the additional offerings, and a time that is fit to occur later within that same day is not considered a lack of time. But the lottery, even though it is not itself an act performed on their bodies, for we have said that the rising of the lot from the container is what is indispensable,

while merely placing the lot down is not indispensable, nevertheless, since it is a mitzvah stated regarding them, it is treated as though it were a lack of an act. 'Now that Rav Chisda has said that lacking the lottery is treated like lacking

an act' - even though it is not itself an act performed on their bodies, for if they were not fit for the additional goat-offering, he would not be liable for slaughtering them outside. 'That which Shmuel said,'

etc. - that lacking the opening of the Sanctuary doors is likewise treated like lacking an act, even though it is not itself an act performed on the bodies of the peace-offerings, since it is stated regarding them, it is treated as though it were an act performed on their bodies.

'But does' - the comment is truncated here; it continues on 63a as 'Rav Chisda really accept the principle of hoil,' challenging whether Rav Chisda's reasoning here is consistent with his position elsewhere.
